guide.title: Overview
guide.markdown:
Python client for the TestBench API. Built for automated test frameworks:
list the fleet, take a device for the duration of a run, record what happened.

```python
from testbench_client import TestBench

with TestBench.from_env() as tb:
    with tb.devices.reserved("dev-0042", purpose="Automated suite", due="2026-12-31") as device:
        passed, metrics = run_my_suite(device.wan_ip)
        tb.tests.record(device, "curl-smoke", passed, misc_data=metrics)
```

The device is checked back in when the block ends — including when it ends by
raising, which is the case that otherwise leaves hardware stranded as
`checked_out` while someone works out who has it.

guide.title: Install
guide.markdown:
```bash
pip install -e src/python-client        # from a checkout
pip install testbench-client   # once it is published
```

One dependency: `httpx`. Python 3.10+.

The client is versioned with TestBench: client 1.15.0 covers everything a
1.15.0 server offers, and still works against older servers for whatever they
have.

guide.title: Authenticating
guide.markdown:
Mint an API key in the web app under **Profile → API keys** and export it. The
full key is shown once, at creation.

```bash
export TB_API_URL=http://localhost:8001   # /api/v1 is appended if you omit it
export TB_API_KEY=tb_1ba207b36474_...
```

```python
tb = TestBench.from_env()                       # reads those two variables
tb = TestBench("http://localhost:8001", key)    # or pass them directly
```

Pick the **lowest role that does the job**. Reading needs no permission at all;
checking a device out needs `devices.edit` and recording a result needs
`tests.edit`. A key never grants more than its owner does, and it can be revoked
from the same page without disturbing the account it belongs to — so give each
framework its own and label it.

Roles are defined per installation, so the role's *name* tells you nothing
portable: check the permissions. `tb.identity` carries both, and is worth
asserting at the top of a run rather than discovering an hour in:

```python
from testbench_client import DEVICES_EDIT, TESTS_EDIT

if not tb.identity.can_write:                   # tests.edit and devices.edit
    sys.exit(f"key is {tb.identity.role}, which cannot run a suite")

if not tb.identity.can(TESTS_EDIT):             # or ask for one permission
    sys.exit("this key cannot record results")
```

An older TestBench that predates definable roles reports only a role name;
`can()` answers from what those three fixed roles granted, so this keeps
working against one.

guide.title: Devices
guide.markdown:
Addressed by `unique_id` ("dev-0042") everywhere. UUIDs work in the same place
but you never need one.

```python
tb.devices.list()                              # the whole fleet, all pages
tb.devices.list(status="available")            # available / checked_out / inventory / missing / broken
tb.devices.list(location="Lab A", limit=10)
tb.devices.list(search="mikrotik")             # unique_id, make, model, location, IPs
tb.devices.iter()                              # same, streamed instead of buffered

device = tb.devices.get("dev-0042")            # detail record, with test history
device.wan_ip, device.architecture, device.firmware_version
device.online                                  # from network scanning
device.is_available, device.is_checked_out     # from the workflow status
device.tests                                   # every recorded run against it
```

`status` and `online` are unrelated: a checked-out device can be answering
pings, and an available one can be dark.

Every timestamp comes back timezone-aware in UTC, so comparing one to
`datetime.now(timezone.utc)` works rather than raising.

guide.title: Checking devices in and out
guide.markdown:
```python
tb.devices.check_out("dev-0042", purpose="Testing", due="2026-12-31")               # raises DeviceUnavailable if taken
tb.devices.check_out("dev-0042", purpose="Testing", due="2026-12-31", force=True)   # admins: take it over
tb.devices.check_in("dev-0042")
tb.devices.set_status("dev-0042", "broken")    # any status, plus other fields

with tb.devices.reserved("dev-0042", purpose="Automated suite", due="2026-12-31") as device:
    ...                                        # released however the block ends
```

Every checkout requires a purpose and return date; choose a date appropriate to your run.

Checking out a device you already hold is not an error, so retries and reruns
are safe.

**Someone else's checkout is theirs.** The API refuses (409) to check out a
device another user holds. `check_out()` reads the device first and raises
`DeviceUnavailable` naming the holder; if another run claims it between that
read and the checkout, the API's refusal — or the re-read afterwards — raises
the same way rather than letting your suite proceed on hardware it does not own.
Only the holder or an admin can check it back in or change its status.
`force=True` takes the device over, which only an admin may do: the checkout
becomes yours in one step, the audit log records it as a take-over, and the
previous holder is notified. Anyone else gets `PermissionDenied`.

That is a guard, not a lock. Two clients calling it at the same instant can
still both pass the API's check. If the hardware is genuinely contended,
serialise somewhere that has a real lock to offer — a CI job queue, a pytest
resource plugin — and use this to record the outcome.

`check_in()` leaves a device alone unless it is checked out *by you*, and
`reserved()` leaves behind any other status the block set. A run that discovered
the device is broken and marked it so does not get that quietly undone on the
way out.

guide.title: Recording results
guide.markdown:
```python
tb.tests.create(
    device="dev-0042",
    software="curl-smoke",          # bare name = the current version
    outcome="pass",                 # pass / fail / warn
    tag="acceptance",               # adhoc / acceptance / end-to-end / automated
    misc_data={"duration_s": 12.4, "mbps": 940, "log": "https://ci/…/42"},
    notes="nightly run",
)

tb.tests.record(device, "curl-smoke", passed=True, misc_data=metrics)   # boolean shorthand
```

`misc_data` is free-form JSON and is the field that makes results worth querying
later — put the numbers there, not in `notes`.

Custom test fields an administrator added under **Schema → Tests** live in
`misc_data` too, by their field key. One marked required has to be there, or
the run is refused with a `ValidationError` naming it (`Lab is required`). To
see what this installation expects:

```python
for field in tb.entity_fields("tests"):
    print(field["key"], field["label"], field["required"])

tb.tests.create(device="dev-0042", software="curl-smoke", outcome="pass",
                misc_data={"lab": "East", "duration_s": 12.4})
tb.tests.list(fields={"lab": "East"})          # filter on any field by key
```

### Suites and components

Software can be a suite of components ("Microsoft 365" with Outlook and
Teams). A run can be recorded against one of them:

```python
suite = tb.software.get("Microsoft 365")
suite.components                                  # [Outlook 16.2, Teams 2.1]
outlook = suite.component("Outlook")

tb.tests.create(device="dev-0042", software=suite, outcome="pass", component=outlook)
# Or by name; a component the suite does not list yet is added to it:
tb.tests.create(device="dev-0042", software="Microsoft 365", outcome="fail",
                component="Word", component_version="16.0")

tb.tests.list(component=outlook)
tb.tests.update(result, component=suite.component("Teams"))   # move a run
```

You pass names; the UUIDs the API wants are resolved and cached for you, so a
suite recording a result per test case makes one request per result rather than
three.

Leaving `software_version` unset records whatever version the software is on
*now*, which is almost always what a run exercised. Pass it explicitly to pin an
older build — an unknown version tells you which ones exist:

```
UnknownSoftware: curl-smoke has no version '0.1'. Known versions: 3.8.6, 3.8.5.
```

Reading results back:

```python
tb.tests.for_device("dev-0042")
tb.tests.list(software="curl-smoke", outcome="fail", limit=20)
tb.tests.update(result, notes="retried, flaky network")
tb.tests.delete(result)
```

### Artifacts and output

A run can carry files: any number of **artifacts** (reports, captures,
screenshots, archives) and one **output** — the run's ASCII text log, which the
TestBench UI shows in a viewer rather than as a download. Both are stored in the
server's object store beside the run, at `tests/<test-id>/artifacts/…` and
`tests/<test-id>/output/…` (inside its test run's folder when it is in one), so
the server needs object storage enabled.

Attach them when recording:

```python
tb.tests.create(
    device="dev-0042", software="curl-smoke", outcome="fail",
    artifacts=["capture.pcap", Path("report.html")],   # paths, bytes or open binary files
    output=log_text,                                     # or output_file="run.log"
)
```

Before recording a run with files, the client asks the server whether it can
store any. If object storage is off, it raises `TestBenchError` and records
nothing, rather than leaving a run behind without the files you meant it to
have. `tb.tests.file_storage()` asks the same question directly, with the size
limits:

```python
storage = tb.tests.file_storage()
storage.enabled, storage.output_max_bytes, storage.artifact_max_bytes
```

Past that check the run is saved first and the files after it. If an upload
fails, the run is still recorded and the exception carries it as `.test`, so
the upload can be retried without recording the run twice.

Or work with a recorded run directly:

```python
tb.tests.upload_artifact(result, "capture.pcap")
tb.tests.upload_artifact(result, png_bytes, filename="screen.png")
for artifact in tb.tests.artifacts(result):
    tb.tests.download_artifact(result, artifact, "downloads/")   # or no dest: returns bytes
tb.tests.delete_artifact(result, artifact)

tb.tests.set_output(result, "all 42 checks passed\n")    # text
tb.tests.upload_output(result, "run.log")                # or a file
print(tb.tests.output(result).text)                       # None when the run has no output
tb.tests.delete_output(result)
```

Output must be ASCII and within the server's limit (1 MiB by default); anything
else is refused with a `ValidationError` before it is stored. Uploading output
again replaces it. A `Test` reports what is attached through `artifact_count`,
`output_filename` and `has_output`. Uploads and deletions need `tests.edit`.

### Test runs

A test run groups the results one pipeline execution recorded, and holds files
that describe the whole execution — a pytest report, say — once, instead of a
copy on every result. Each result in the run lists them beside its own files.

```python
run = tb.test_runs.start(
    f"Nightly #{os.environ['CI_PIPELINE_ID']}",
    external_id=os.environ["CI_PIPELINE_ID"],   # every job of the pipeline joins one run
    url=os.environ["CI_PIPELINE_URL"],
)
tb.test_runs.attach(run, "report.html")          # stored once, shared by every test in the run
for target in targets:
    tb.tests.create(device=target, software="RouterOS", outcome="pass", test_run=run)
tb.test_runs.finish(run)
```

`start()` with an `external_id` already in use returns that run rather than a
new one, so parallel jobs can each call it. Without one, each call starts a new
run.

A test can also share files with its run as it is recorded, which suits a test
recorded by hand, with its outline or report:

```python
run = tb.test_runs.start("Acceptance 2026-10")
tb.tests.create(device="dev-0042", software="RouterOS", outcome="pass", test_run=run,
                artifacts=["capture.pcap"],                # this test's own files
                test_run_artifacts=["test-outline.pdf"])   # shared with every test in the run
```

In GitLab CI or GitHub Actions, `start_from_ci()` fills all of that in from the
pipeline's own environment variables:

```python
run = tb.test_runs.start_from_ci()      # every job of the pipeline gets the same run
```

| | GitLab CI | GitHub Actions |
|---|---|---|
| One run per | pipeline (`CI_PIPELINE_ID`) | workflow run (`GITHUB_RUN_ID`) |
| Name | `group/project #812 (main)` | `owner/repo CI #57 (main)` |
| `external_id` | `gitlab:<host>:<pipeline id>` | `github:<host>:<run id>` |
| Link | `CI_PIPELINE_URL` | the workflow run's page |

Retried GitLab jobs and re-run GitHub jobs keep their pipeline's ID, so their
results join the same run. Pass a name to use your own (`start_from_ci("Nightly
smoke")`); only the job that creates the run sets it. Outside either CI system
it raises `ValueError` — use `start()` there.

```python
tb.test_runs.list(search="nightly")           # newest first
tb.test_runs.get(run_id).fail_count           # test_count, pass_count, fail_count, warn_count
tb.test_runs.tests(run, outcome="fail")       # the run's results; takes tb.tests.list() filters
tb.tests.list(test_run="none")                # results recorded outside any run
tb.tests.shared_artifacts(result)             # the run's files, from one of its results
tb.test_runs.download_artifact(run, artifact, "downloads/")
tb.tests.update(result, test_run=other_run)   # or test_run=None to take it out
tb.test_runs.delete(run)                      # its results are kept, in no run
```

A `Test` names its run in `test_run_id` and `test_run_name`, and counts the
run's shared files in `test_run_artifact_count`.

### One run, one build

A bare software name resolves once per client and stays resolved. If someone
adds a new version halfway through your suite, results keep attaching to the
build the run started against — one run, one set of evidence, rather than a
suite split across two versions at an arbitrary point. Call `tb.clear_cache()`
if you want the opposite.

guide.title: Software
guide.markdown:
Read-only. Recording a result needs software that already exists; a test
framework inventing catalogue rows is how a catalogue fills up with typos.

```python
tb.software.list(latest_only=True)
tb.software.get("curl-smoke")                  # current version
tb.software.get("curl-smoke", "3.8.5")         # a specific one
tb.software.versions("curl-smoke")             # all of them, newest first
tb.software.components("Microsoft 365")        # a suite's components

# Devices this version has actually been run against, from its results:
for entry in tb.software.tested_devices("curl-smoke"):
    print(entry.device.unique_id, entry.test_count, entry.outcomes, entry.component)
```

guide.title: Search
guide.markdown:
The web app's search box, across devices, software, tests and vendor claims at
once. It matches suite components too:

```python
found = tb.search("Outlook", limit=20)
for software in found.software:
    print(software, [c.name for c in software.matching_components])
found.devices_total, found.software_total, found.tests_total, found.vendor_devices_total
```

guide.title: Vendor devices
guide.markdown:
Hardware a vendor **claims** their software supports — their published
compatibility list. These are not the same as `tests`:

- a vendor device is a **claim**. Not evidence, and not necessarily hardware
  this fleet owns.
- a test is **evidence**. Absence of one means untested, not unsupported.

Code that treats them as interchangeable is the mistake this section exists to
prevent; `tb.vendor_devices.for_device(...)` and `tb.tests.for_device(...)`
answer different questions and routinely disagree.

```python
# Every compatibility list at once — the question no single software answers.
tb.vendor_devices.list(search="ISR 4331")
tb.vendor_devices.list(make="Cisco", support_status="supported")
matches = tb.vendor_devices.list(
    model="R1", component_name="Outlook", component_version="16.2",
    component_status="supported",
)
for claim in matches:
    print(claim.matching_components)  # effective status and inherited flag

# One software's own list. A bare name gives the current version's.
tb.vendor_devices.for_software("curl-smoke")
tb.vendor_devices.for_software("curl-smoke", "3.8.5")

# Who claims to support a device in the fleet, found by its make and model.
for claim in tb.vendor_devices.for_device("dev-0042", supported_only=True):
    print(claim)        # Cisco ISR 4331: supported (Backup-Restore 2.0)

# The same question answered the way the device page answers it, one entry
# per software version. Broader: a claim naming only a make matches.
for match in tb.devices.compatible_software("dev-0042"):
    print(match.software, match.support_status, match.matched_on, match.claims)

# And the other way round: which devices in the fleet a claim describes.
claim = tb.vendor_devices.list(make="Cisco")[0]
claim.inventory_match_count, claim.inventory_devices   # count, first few
tb.vendor_devices.inventory_matches(claim)             # every unique ID
```

Every row names the software and version making the claim. `software_is_latest`
is false for a claim made by a version that has since been superseded — still a
real claim, but not current guidance:

```python
current = [c for c in tb.vendor_devices.for_device("dev-0042") if c.software_is_latest]
```

`support_status` is the vendor's own word — `supported`, `partial`,
`unsupported` or `planned`. Unsupported rows come back like any other, because
"the vendor says no" is an answer; `supported_only=` and `.is_supported` filter
to the unqualified yes.
`component_status` filters the effective status of the same named component
version, falling back to the suite status when that component has no explicit
override. It describes a vendor claim, not a recorded test result.

To import claims, use one row per component. Each row must include the software
name and version plus the same hardware fields for claims that should merge.
The API key needs `software.edit`:

```python
tb.vendor_devices.import_csv("vendor-claims.csv")
# Or pass dictionaries directly:
tb.vendor_devices.import_rows([
    {"software_name": "Microsoft 365", "software_version": "2026.1",
     "make": "Acme", "model": "R1", "component_name": "Outlook",
     "component_version": "16.2", "component_status": "supported"},
    {"software_name": "Microsoft 365", "software_version": "2026.1",
     "make": "Acme", "model": "R1", "component_name": "Teams",
     "component_version": "2.1", "component_status": "unsupported"},
])
```

Both methods return `created`, `updated`, and `errors`. The older
`component_support` list also remains accepted.

guide.title: Errors
guide.markdown:
Every exception subclasses `TestBenchError` and carries `.status` and
`.detail`. The API's own `detail` strings are passed through rather than
replaced — they usually say what to do next.

| Exception | When |
|---|---|
| `AuthenticationError` | 401 — key missing, expired or revoked |
| `PermissionDenied` | 403 — the key's role is too low |
| `NotFound` / `UnknownDevice` / `UnknownSoftware` | 404, the latter two with `.suggestions` |
| `Conflict` / `DeviceUnavailable` | the device is held, or not available |
| `ValidationError` | 400/422 |
| `ServerError` | 5xx |
| `TransportError` | never reached the API |

`UnknownDevice` includes near misses, which is usually enough to spot a typo
from a CI log alone:

```
UnknownDevice: No device 'dev-00'. Did you mean: dev-0001, dev-0002, dev-0003?
```

Bad enum values are caught before the request goes out. This matters more than
it looks: the API does not validate *filter* values, so `status="braken"`
returns an empty page — which reads as "there are no broken devices". A wrong
answer is worse than an error.

guide.title: Retries
guide.markdown:
GETs retry twice through transport failures and 5xx, with jittered backoff.
Writes are never retried: a `POST /tests` that may have landed must not be sent
twice, because a duplicate result is worse than a failure you can see. 401 and
403 are never retried either — a revoked key does not become valid by asking
again.

Tune with `TestBench(..., retries=0)`.

guide.title: Concurrency
guide.markdown:
`httpx.Client` is thread-safe and the resolution cache is locked, so one client
can be shared across threads. Prefer one per process: it holds the connection
pool and the cache, which is most of why this is faster than shelling out to
curl. Under `pytest-xdist` each worker is its own process and gets its own.

guide.title: Examples
guide.markdown:
- `examples/inventory.py` — the fleet, grouped by status
- `examples/run_suite.py` — reserve, run, record
- `examples/coverage_gap.py` — vendor claims with no test evidence behind them
- `examples/pytest_conftest.py` — fixtures that reserve a device for a session
  and record a result per test from its actual outcome

guide.title: Not included
guide.markdown:
- Creating or editing devices and software — `POST /devices`, `POST /software`
  and friends exist; they are deliberately not wrapped, because an automated
  framework should be recording evidence, not editing the inventory.
- Bulk and CSV import (`/devices/import`, `/tests/import`).
- Saved filters, users, roles, audit log.

Each is a short method following the pattern in `devices.py` if you need it.

guide.title: A note on the audit log
guide.markdown:
Actions taken with an API key are audited under the owner's username with the
key's id and label attached. Two consequences worth knowing: results recorded by
your framework are attributed to a person, and revoking a key answers "what did
it do?" and not only "who owned it?". Label keys so that stays useful.

reference.doc:
A connection to a TestBench instance.

```python
from testbench_client import TestBench

with TestBench.from_env() as tb:
    for device in tb.devices.list(status="available"):
        print(device)
```

Safe to share between threads: `httpx.Client` is thread-safe and the name
resolution cache is locked. Prefer one client per process — each holds a
connection pool, and reusing it is most of why this is faster than curl.

members.name: entity_fields
members.doc:
Logical device/software/test fields this installation exposes.

With no argument, every entity's fields by entity name. With one —
"software", "tests" or "vendor_devices" — that entity's list alone,
each field with its key, label, type, and whether it is `visible` and
`required`. A custom field marked required has to be in a record's
`misc_data` for the server to accept it.

The device entry is the *global* device schema — the fields every
device type inherits. For one type's own fields, use
`device_schema(type_key)`.

members.name: search
members.doc:
Search devices, software, tests and vendor claims at once, as the
web app's search box does.

Matches suite components too: software comes back with the
`matching_components` that matched, and devices with the
`tested_components` that did. `limit` caps each group (at most 200).

members.name: device_types
members.doc: The inventory categories this installation defines.

members.name: device_schema
members.doc:
The published schema for one device type, or the global one.

What a device of this type looks like here: which fields it carries, in
what order, which are required, and which plugins may act on it. Field
keys are stable and are what every other call in this library uses;
labels are presentation only.

members.name: device_schema_revision
members.doc: The published revision, for a caller that caches schemas.

members.name: from_env
members.doc:
Build a client from `TB_API_URL` and `TB_API_KEY`.

The usual shape for CI, where the key is an injected secret and nothing
should be reading it out of a checked-in config file.

members.name: whoami
members.doc:
The account and effective role this key resolves to.

Worth calling once at the start of a run: it turns a revoked key into
one clear failure at setup instead of a confusing one an hour into a
suite. The result is cached; pass refresh=True to re-check.

members.name: request
members.signature: (method: str, path: str, *, params: dict | None = None, json: Any = None, files: dict | None = None) -> Any
members.doc:
Make one API call and return parsed JSON (None for 204).

Retries idempotent requests through transport failures and 5xx; a
response the API meant to send is never retried, because a 403 does not
become a 200 by asking again.

members.name: clear_cache
members.doc:
Forget resolved names.

Call this if software gained a new version mid-run and you want bare
names to start meaning the new one. See `software.resolve()` for why
that is otherwise sticky on purpose.

reference.init_signature: (base_url: str | None = None, api_key: str | None = None, *, timeout: float = 30.0, retries: int = 2, verify: bool | str = True, page_size: int = 200, transport: httpx.BaseTransport | None = None) -> None

reference.doc:
Accessed as `tb.devices`.

Devices are addressed by their `unique_id` ("dev-0042") everywhere in this
library. The API accepts a UUID in the same position, so either works, but
nothing here requires you to know one.

members.name: list
members.signature: (*, search: str | None = None, device_type: str | None = None, status: str | None = None, location: str | None = None, overdue: bool | None = None, fields: dict[str, str | int | float | bool] | None = None, sort: str = 'unique_id', order: str = 'asc', limit: int | None = None) -> list[Device]
members.doc:
Every device matching the filters, across as many pages as it takes.

With no filters this is the whole fleet. `limit` caps the rows fetched,
not just the rows returned — it stops paging early.

`overdue=True` narrows to devices past their return date; False to
everything else. `device_type` takes a stable type key — "router",
"mobile", or "uncategorized" for devices with no type — never a label,
which an administrator may rename at any time.

`fields` filters on any field this installation defines, by its stable
key: `fields={"serial_number": "SN-1"}`.

members.name: iter
members.signature: (*, search: str | None = None, device_type: str | None = None, status: str | None = None, location: str | None = None, overdue: bool | None = None, fields: dict[str, str | int | float | bool] | None = None, sort: str = 'unique_id', order: str = 'asc', limit: int | None = None) -> Iterator[Device]
members.doc: Like `list()`, but yields as pages arrive rather than buffering.

members.name: overdue
members.signature: (*, min_days: int = 1, limit: int | None = None) -> list[Device]
members.doc:
Devices past their return date, longest overdue first.

The dedicated endpoint rather than `list(overdue=True)`: it sorts by how
late each one is, which is the order you want when the list is a queue
of people to go and ask.

members.name: get
members.doc:
One device by unique_id (or UUID), with its test history attached.

This is the detail record: `device.tests` and `device.verified_tests`
are populated, which `list()` does not do.

members.name: actions
members.doc:
Plugin actions for one device, each saying whether it can run.

Not every installed action applies to every device: a plugin is
available only where the device type's policy allows it and the fields
it needs are both configured and filled in. Each entry carries
`available` and, when it is false, `unavailable_reason`.

members.name: compatible_software
members.doc:
Software whose vendor claims describe this device, as its page shows.

The server's own matching, which is broader than `vendor_devices.for_device()`:
a claim pinning only the make matches every device of that make, and
firmware, hardware version and architecture are compared too when the
claim names them. Each entry is one software version with its matching
claims and how well they fit (`matched_on`).

Claims, not evidence: what has actually run here is `tests.for_device()`.

members.name: schema
members.doc: The published schema for this device's type.

members.name: resolve
members.doc:
The device's UUID, which `POST /tests` needs and people do not have.

Cached for the life of the client: a device's id never changes, and a
suite recording a result per test case would otherwise re-fetch the
same row hundreds of times.

members.name: set_status
members.doc:
Set a device's status, and optionally other fields in the same call.

Crossing into `checked_out` stamps the key owner and the day; crossing
out of it clears them, along with the purpose and the return date. That
happens server-side — this does not, and cannot, set `checked_out_by`
itself.

Note that entering `checked_out` needs `checkout_purpose` and
`checkout_due` passed as fields, or the API returns 422. `check_out()`
is the method that gets that right.

members.name: check_out
members.signature: (identifier: str | Device, *, purpose: str, due: date | str, force: bool = False) -> Device
members.doc:
Take the device, refusing if it is not free.

`purpose` and `due` are required, because the API requires them: a
checkout has to say why the device is out and when it is coming back.
Past `due` the device shows as overdue and whoever holds it is
reminded daily — nothing takes it back automatically.

The API refuses (409) a checkout of a device someone else holds, and
this checks first as well, so the refusal comes back as
`DeviceUnavailable` naming the holder. `force=True` takes it over
instead — an admin's call only; anyone else gets `PermissionDenied`. If another run claimed it between
the check and the checkout, that 409 — or the re-read afterwards —
raises the same way, rather than letting a suite proceed on hardware it
does not own.

That is a guard, not a lock: two clients calling this at the same
instant can both pass the API's check. For genuinely contended
hardware, serialise at a level that has a lock to offer (a CI job
queue, a resource plugin).

Already holding it is not an error — this is safe to call twice.

members.name: check_in
members.signature: (identifier: str | Device, *, only_if_mine: bool = True) -> Device
members.doc:
Return the device to `available`.

Idempotent: a device that is not checked out is left exactly as it is,
including one someone deliberately marked `broken` — an automated
release should not quietly undo that.

`only_if_mine=False` returns someone else's checkout, which the API
allows only an admin; anyone else gets `DeviceUnavailable`.

members.name: reserved
members.signature: (identifier: str | Device, *, purpose: str, due: date | str, force: bool = False)
members.doc:
Hold a device for the duration of a block, and always give it back.

```python
with tb.devices.reserved("dev-0042", purpose="Nightly suite",
                         due=date.today() + timedelta(days=1)) as device:
    run_the_suite_against(device.wan_ip)
```

The purpose and return date are the ones every checkout needs. For a
block that gives the device back at the end, a date a day or two out is
the honest answer: it is what the fleet should show if the block never
reaches its release.

The release runs even if the block raises, which is the entire point:
a crashed run that strands hardware as `checked_out` costs someone an
afternoon of wondering who has it.

If the block leaves the device in some other state — `broken`, say,
because that is what the run discovered — the release leaves it there.

reference.doc:
Accessed as `tb.software`.

Named `SoftwareResource` rather than `Software` so it does not collide with
the record class of that name; you never write the class name yourself.

members.name: list
members.signature: (*, search: str | None = None, latest_only: bool = False, fields: dict[str, str | int | float | bool] | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> list[Software]

Software in the catalogue. `latest_only` collapses version groups to

members.signature: (*, search: str | None = None, latest_only: bool = False, fields: dict[str, str | int | float | bool] | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> Iterator[Software]

members.signature: (name: str | Software, version: str | None = None) -> Software
members.doc:
One piece of software by name (or UUID).

A bare name gives the CURRENT version — the highest numeric version.
Pass `version` for a specific one.

members.name: versions
members.doc: Every version sharing this name, newest first.

members.name: components
members.signature: (name: str | Software, version: str | None = None) -> list[SoftwareComponent]
members.doc:
The components of a software suite at one version (current by default).

Empty for software that is not a suite. Pass one to
`tests.create(component=...)` to record a run against it.

members.name: tested_devices
members.signature: (name: str | Software, version: str | None = None, *, search: str | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> list[TestedDevice]
members.doc:
Devices this software version has actually been tested on, from its runs.

One entry per device (per component, for a suite), with how many runs
there were, the outcome counts and the latest run date. Evidence, unlike
`vendor_devices.for_software()`, which is what the vendor claims.

members.name: resolve
members.signature: (name: str | Software, version: str | None = None) -> str
members.doc:
The software's UUID, which `POST /tests` needs.

Cached for the life of the client. For a bare name that means the run
keeps recording against whichever version was current when the first
result was written, even if someone adds a new version halfway through
— which is what you want from a test run: one build, one set of
evidence. Call `tb.clear_cache()` if you want the opposite.

members.name: create
members.signature: (*, device: str | Device, software: str | Software, outcome: str, tag: str = 'adhoc', software_version: str | None = None, component: str | SoftwareComponent | None = None, component_version: str | None = None, misc_data: dict | None = None, notes: str | None = None, run_at: date | str | None = None, test_run: str | TestRun | None = None, test_run_artifacts: Iterable[FileSource] | None = None, artifacts: Iterable[FileSource] | None = None, output: str | None = None, output_file: FileSource | None = None) -> Test
members.doc:
Record one run, optionally with its files.

```python
tb.tests.create(device="dev-0042", software="nmap", outcome="pass",
                tag="acceptance", misc_data={"duration_s": 12.4})
```

`device` and `software` are the names you already have; the UUIDs the
API wants are resolved and cached for you.

Leaving `software_version` unset records the version the software is on
now, which is almost always right — the run exercised whatever is
current. Set it when the run exercised a build the catalogue has moved
past.

`component` records the run against one component of a software suite
("Outlook" in "Microsoft 365"): a `SoftwareComponent` from
`software.components`, or its name with `component_version`. A name the
suite does not list yet is added to it, as the web app does.

`misc_data` is free-form JSON: durations, throughput, log URLs, exit codes.
It is the field that makes these results worth querying later, so put
the numbers in it rather than in `notes`. Custom test fields an
administrator defined under Schema -> Tests live in it too, by their
field key; one marked required has to be there or the run is refused
with a ValidationError naming it. `tb.entity_fields("tests")` lists them.

`test_run` puts the run in a test run (a `TestRun` from
`tb.test_runs.start()`, or its id), whose shared files, such as a
pytest report, then show with this run's own. Its own files are
stored in the test run's folder in the bucket.

`test_run_artifacts` shares files with every test in that run, such as
a report or a test outline, as `tb.test_runs.attach()` does; it needs
`test_run`. Attach a file once per run, not with every test.

`artifacts` attaches files (paths, bytes or open binary files) and
`output` the run's text output — or `output_file` to read it from disk.
When there are files, the server is asked first whether it can store
any (`file_storage()`), so a run is never recorded with files that were
always going to be refused. Past that, the run is recorded first and the
files uploaded after it, so an upload that fails leaves the run
recorded: the exception carries it as `.test`, for a retry with
`upload_artifact()` or `set_output()`.

members.name: record
members.doc:
`create()` for the common case where a framework has a boolean.

Maps True to "pass" and False to "fail". "warn" has no boolean, so
reach for `create()` when you want it.

members.name: update
members.doc:
Amend a recorded result (outcome, tag, misc_data, notes, run_at,
software_version).

`component=` moves the run onto another component of its suite; it
takes a `SoftwareComponent` or a component id, since the API amends by
id only.

`test_run=` moves the run into a test run (a `TestRun` or its id), and
`test_run=None` takes it out of one. Files already uploaded stay where
they were stored.

members.name: list
members.signature: (*, device: str | Device | None = None, software: str | Software | None = None, software_version: str | None = None, outcome: str | None = None, tag: str | None = None, component: str | SoftwareComponent | None = None, component_version: str | None = None, test_run: str | TestRun | None = None, search: str | None = None, fields: dict[str, str | int | float | bool] | None = None, sort: str = 'created_at', order: str = 'desc', limit: int | None = None) -> list[Test]
members.doc:
Recorded runs, newest first, across as many pages as it takes.

`component` and `component_version` narrow to runs recorded against a
suite component. `test_run` narrows to one test run's (a `TestRun` or
its id); `test_run="none"` to runs recorded outside any. `fields` filters on any test field by its key,
including custom ones: `fields={"lab": "East"}`.

members.name: iter
members.signature: (*, device: str | Device | None = None, software: str | Software | None = None, software_version: str | None = None, outcome: str | None = None, tag: str | None = None, component: str | SoftwareComponent | None = None, component_version: str | None = None, test_run: str | TestRun | None = None, search: str | None = None, fields: dict[str, str | int | float | bool] | None = None, sort: str = 'created_at', order: str = 'desc', limit: int | None = None) -> Iterator[Test]

members.name: for_device
members.signature: (device: str | Device, *, limit: int | None = None) -> list[Test]
members.doc: Every recorded run against one device, newest first.

members.name: file_storage
members.doc:
Whether this server can store output and artifacts, and the limits.

Both live in object storage an administrator configures; without it,
uploads are refused. A server older than 1.13.4 cannot say, and is
reported as enabled with no known limits — the upload itself is then
what finds out.

members.name: artifacts
shared_artifacts
members.doc:
The files the run's test run shares with all of its tests, such as a
pytest report. Empty for a run outside any test run. Download them with
`tb.test_runs.download_artifact()`.

members.name: upload_artifact
members.signature: (test: str | Test, file: FileSource, *, filename: str | None = None, content_type: str | None = None) -> TestArtifact
members.doc:
Attach one file to a run. Repeat for more; duplicate names are fine.

```python
tb.tests.upload_artifact(result, "capture.pcap")
tb.tests.upload_artifact(result, png_bytes, filename="screen.png")
```

Needs `tests.edit`, and object storage enabled on the server.

members.name: download_artifact
members.signature: (test: str | Test, artifact: str | TestArtifact, dest: str | os.PathLike[str] | BinaryIO | None = None) -> bytes | Path | None
members.doc:
Fetch an artifact's bytes.

With no `dest`, returns the bytes. With a directory, saves under the
artifact's own filename (which needs the `TestArtifact`, not just its
id) and returns the path; with a file path, saves there and returns it;
with an open binary file, writes into it and returns None.

members.name: delete_artifact
members.signature: (test: str | Test, artifact: str | TestArtifact) -> None

members.name: output
members.doc: The run's text output, or None when it has none.

members.name: set_output
members.signature: (test: str | Test, text: str, *, filename: str = 'output.txt') -> TestOutput
members.doc:
Store `text` as the run's output, replacing any it had.

Output is ASCII text the TestBench UI shows in a viewer; anything else is
refused with a ValidationError, as is a file over the server's limit
(1 MiB unless configured otherwise).

members.name: upload_output
members.signature: (test: str | Test, file: FileSource, *, filename: str | None = None) -> TestOutput
members.doc: Store a file (path, bytes or open binary file) as the run's output.

members.name: delete_output
members.doc: Remove the run's output. Raises NotFound when it has none.

members.name: start
members.signature: (name: str, *, external_id: str | None = None, url: str | None = None, started_at: datetime | str | None = None, notes: str | None = None) -> TestRun
members.doc:
Start a test run, or join the one already started with `external_id`.

Pass the CI pipeline's ID as `external_id` and every job of the
pipeline can call this and get the same run back, whichever starts
first; the first caller's name and link are the ones kept. Without
one, every call starts a run of its own. `started_at` defaults to now.

members.name: start_from_ci
members.signature: (name: str | None = None, *, notes: str | None = None, env: Mapping[str, str] | None = None) -> TestRun
members.doc:
Start, or join, the test run for the CI pipeline this is running in.

Reads GitLab CI or GitHub Actions' own environment variables for the
pipeline's ID, link and a name, so every job of one pipeline gets the
same run without passing anything:

```python
run = tb.test_runs.start_from_ci()
```

- GitLab: one run per pipeline (`CI_PIPELINE_ID`), named like
  `group/project #812 (main)` and linked to `CI_PIPELINE_URL`. Retried
  jobs stay in the pipeline, so their results join the same run.
- GitHub Actions: one run per workflow run (`GITHUB_RUN_ID`), named like
  `owner/repo CI #57 (main)` and linked to the run's page. Re-running
  jobs keeps the run ID, so their results join the same run too.

The external ID is prefixed with the CI system and its host
(`gitlab:gitlab.example.com:812`), so pipelines from two systems never
share a run. `name` overrides the generated name, which only the job
that creates the run gets to set. Raises ValueError outside either CI
system; use `start()` there. `env` defaults to `os.environ`.

members.name: update
members.doc: Change a run's name, external_id, url, notes, started_at or finished_at.

members.signature: (run: str | TestRun, *, at: datetime | str | None = None) -> TestRun
members.doc: Mark the run finished, now unless `at` says when.

members.name: delete
members.doc: Delete the run. Its tests are kept, no longer in a run.

members.name: list
members.signature: (*, search: str | None = None, sort: str = 'created_at', order: str = 'desc', limit: int | None = None) -> list[TestRun]
members.doc: Test runs, newest first. `search` matches the name or external_id.

Share a file (path, bytes or open binary file) with every test in the run.

Stored once, in the run's folder in the bucket. Needs `tests.edit`, and

Fetch a shared file: bytes with no `dest`, else saved as

reference.doc:
Accessed as `tb.vendor_devices`.

Searches every software version's compatibility list at once. To read one
software's list on its own, pass `software=`.

members.name: import_rows
members.doc:
Import vendor claims across software versions.

Each row needs `software_name`, `software_version`, and hardware fields.
Use `component_name`, `component_version`, and optional
`component_status` for one component per row. Rows for the same
software version and hardware merge their component claims. The server
reports `created`, `updated`, and per-row `errors`.

members.name: import_csv
members.doc: Upload a Vendor Claims CSV, including flat component columns.

members.name: list
members.signature: (*, search: str | None = None, software: str | Software | None = None, make: str | None = None, model: str | None = None, firmware_version: str | None = None, hardware_version: str | None = None, architecture: str | None = None, support_status: str | None = None, component_name: str | None = None, component_version: str | None = None, component_status: str | None = None, sort: str = 'make', order: str = 'asc', limit: int | None = None) -> list[VendorDevice]
members.doc:
Every claim matching the filters, across as many pages as it takes.

`search` matches make, model, firmware, hardware version, architecture,
source, notes, component names and versions, and the software's own
name and version at once; the
named filters are narrower and combine with AND.

`software` takes a name and covers **every version of it** — a claim
made by 1.0 and one made by 2.0 are separate rows, and both come back.
Use `for_software()` to read one version's list on its own.

`support_status` filters the general vendor claim: supported, partial,
unsupported or planned. Per-component overrides are available on each
returned row's `component_support` list. Component filters match one
component version's effective status; `matching_components` identifies
each match and whether it inherited the suite status.

members.name: iter
members.signature: (*, search: str | None = None, software: str | Software | None = None, make: str | None = None, model: str | None = None, firmware_version: str | None = None, hardware_version: str | None = None, architecture: str | None = None, support_status: str | None = None, component_name: str | None = None, component_version: str | None = None, component_status: str | None = None, sort: str = 'make', order: str = 'asc', limit: int | None = None) -> Iterator[VendorDevice]
members.doc: Like `list()`, but yields as pages arrive rather than buffering.

members.name: for_software
members.signature: (name: str | Software, version: str | None = None, *, search: str | None = None, support_status: str | None = None, component_name: str | None = None, component_version: str | None = None, component_status: str | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> list[VendorDevice]
members.doc:
One software version's own compatibility list.

A bare name gives the current version's list, the same way every other
name in this library resolves. Note that versions do not inherit from
one another: a new version starts as a copy and the two diverge, so
this is genuinely the list that version publishes — not its ancestor's.

Resolved to an id and asked of the catalogue rather than of the
software's own sub-resource: the catalogue takes the same filters as
`list()` and its rows already name the software they belong to, so a
record is the same shape whichever way it arrived.

members.name: for_device
members.signature: (identifier: str | Device, *, supported_only: bool = False, component_name: str | None = None, component_version: str | None = None, component_status: str | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> list[VendorDevice]
members.doc:
Claims describing a device in the fleet, by its own make and model.

A convenience over `list()`, not a new question: it reads the device's
make and model and searches the catalogue for them. Claims are matched
on the hardware a vendor published, so a claim naming only a make will
not be found by a search that also pins the model — this errs towards
the narrow answer, which is the one that is actually about this device.

Returns nothing for a device with neither a make nor a model; there is
nothing to match on, and every claim in the catalogue is not an answer.

members.name: inventory_matches
members.signature: (claim: VendorDevice, *, limit: int | None = None) -> list[str]
members.doc:
Unique IDs of the devices in the fleet this claim describes.

`claim.inventory_devices` holds only the first few; this pages through
all of them. Matched the same way the claims list counts them.

models.name: Device
models.doc:
A device in the fleet.

`status` is the workflow state a person sets; `online` comes from network
scanning and is unrelated — a checked-out device can be online, and an
available one offline.

members.name: field
members.doc:
One installation-defined value, by its stable field key.

Keys are stable; labels are presentation and may be changed by an
administrator at any time, so nothing here is addressed by label.

members.name: is_overdue
members.doc:
Past its return date and still out.

Derived here the same way the API derives it, so a Device read from any
endpoint can answer without a second call.

members.name: days_overdue
members.doc: How many days late, or 0 if it is not.

models.name: DeviceType
models.doc: One inventory category, with its own page, columns and rules.

models.name: Software
models.doc:
A piece of software at one version.

Rows sharing a name are one software; a bare name always addresses the
CURRENT version, which is the highest numeric version in its name group.

members.name: is_suite
members.doc: Whether this version is made of components.

members.name: component
members.signature: (name: str, version: str | None = None) -> SoftwareComponent | None
members.doc: One of this version's components by name (any case), or None.

models.name: SoftwareComponent
models.doc:
One component of a software suite at one version: "Outlook 16.2" in
"Microsoft 365 2026.1".

A suite version lists its components; a test can be recorded against one of
them, and a vendor claim can say something different about one of them than
about the suite as a whole.

models.name: Test
models.doc:
One recorded run of a piece of software against a device.

`software_version` is a snapshot taken when the run was recorded, not a
live reference: the software moves on, the evidence stays attached to the
build it was gathered on.

models.name: TestArtifact
models.doc:
A file attached to a recorded run: a report, a capture, a screenshot.

Stored privately in the server's object store under
`tests/<test-id>/artifacts/<artifact-id>/<filename>`, or inside its test
run's folder when the test belongs to one; download it with
`tb.tests.download_artifact()`.

models.name: TestedDevice
models.doc:
A device a software version has actually been run against, from its tests.

Evidence, unlike a vendor claim. With a suite, each component tested on a
device is its own entry, naming the `component`.

fields.name: device
fields.default: Device(id='', unique_id='', device_type_id=None, device_type_key=None, device_type_label=None, status='', location=None, make=None, model=None, firmware_version=None, hardware_version=None, architecture=None, wan_ip=None, lan_ip=None, online=False, last_seen_online=None, last_scanned_at=None, misc_data={}, checked_out_by=None, checked_out_by_username=None, checked_out_at=None, checkout_purpose=None, checkout_due=None, data={}, link_overrides={}, created_at=None, updated_at=None)

models.name: TestFileStorage
models.doc:
Whether recorded runs can carry files here, and how big.

Output and artifacts both live in the server's object storage. With it
switched off, uploads are refused and reads find nothing.

models.name: TestOutput
models.doc:
A run's one text output file, as read back from the server.

`text` is None when the server could not read the stored file; `error` then
says why (most often that the object has gone from the bucket). The output
can still be replaced or deleted.

models.name: TestRun
models.doc:
One execution of a pipeline or suite: the tests it recorded, and the
files it shares with all of them, such as a pytest report, stored once.

`external_id` is the caller's own identity for the run, such as a CI
pipeline ID; starting a run with one already in use joins that run.

models.name: TestRunArtifact
models.doc:
A file a test run shares with every test in it.

Stored once, under `test-runs/<run-name>_<run-id>/artifacts/` in the
server's object store, and listed with each of the run's tests.

models.name: VendorDevice
models.doc:
Hardware a vendor CLAIMS their software supports.

Not a device in the fleet and not evidence: a row here says a vendor
published support for that hardware, whether or not anyone owns one and
whether or not it has ever been run. What has actually been tested is a
`Test`, and absence of one means untested, not unsupported.

A claim belongs to one software version, which `software_name` and
`software_version` name. `software_is_latest` is false for a claim made by
a version that has since been superseded — still a real claim, but not
current guidance.

members.name: is_supported
members.doc: The vendor said yes without qualification. `partial` is not this.

members.name: hardware
members.doc: Make and model as one string, for a log line.

models.name: CompatibleSoftware
models.doc:
A software version whose vendor claims describe one device.

Answers "who claims to support this box?", matched the way the device page
matches it. Still a claim, not evidence: see `VendorDevice`.

fields.name: software
fields.default: Software(id='', name='', version='', version_count=1, is_latest=True, vendor_device_count=0, misc_data={}, components=[], bundle_parent_count=0, matching_components=[], created_at=None, updated_at=None)

models.name: SearchResults
models.doc:
What the web app's search box finds for one query, grouped by kind.

Each list holds at most the limit asked for; the totals count every match.

models.name: Identity
models.doc: Who the configured API key authenticates as, and what it may do.

members.name: can
members.doc:
Whether this key holds one permission, e.g. `can(TESTS_EDIT)`.

Worth asking at the start of a run rather than discovering it as a 403
halfway through a suite.

members.name: can_write
members.doc:
Whether this key may record results and check devices out.

The two things a test framework does. A key that can do one and not the
other is unusual but expressible, and this is deliberately the
conjunction: a suite that can check a device out and then cannot write
down what happened has failed in the least useful way possible.

errors.name: TestBenchError
errors.doc:
Base for everything this library raises.

Catching this catches every failure the client can produce, including the
ones that never reached the API.

errors.name: TransportError
errors.doc:
The request never reached the API, or no response came back.

Not named ConnectionError: that is a builtin, and shadowing it in a library
people will `from ... import *` is a trap.

errors.name: AuthenticationError
errors.doc:
401 — the API key is missing, malformed, expired or revoked.

Never retried. A key does not become valid again on its own; something has
to mint a new one.

errors.name: PermissionDenied
errors.doc:
403 — authenticated, but the key's role is too low for this call.

A key's role is the lower of the role it was minted with and its owner's
current role, so this can appear without the key itself changing.

errors.name: NotFound
errors.doc: 404 — no such device, test or software.

errors.name: Conflict
errors.doc: 409 — the request collided with the current state.

errors.name: ValidationError
errors.doc: 400 or 422 — the request body or query was rejected.

errors.name: UnknownDevice
errors.doc:
No device matched the identifier given.

`suggestions` holds near misses from a search on the same string, which is
usually enough to spot a typo from a CI log alone.

errors.name: UnknownSoftware
errors.doc: No software matched the name (or the name matched, but not that version).

errors.name: DeviceUnavailable
errors.doc:
The device cannot be checked out: someone else holds it, or it is not
available (broken, missing, in inventory).

Raised by this library, usually before the API is asked at all, so it
carries no HTTP status — except when the API's own 409 caught a device
claimed mid-checkout, which it passes on. `device` is the record as it was
when the attempt was refused.
